chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Commodities Are and Why They Trade

lessons.title: Where Commodities Trade in India: MCX, NCDEX, NSE and BSE

children.text: Open Zerodha Kite or any other broker app, activate the commodity segment, and search "GOLD". You will see contracts from MCX, and possibly from NSE and BSE too. Search "JEERA" and you will be sent to NCDEX. Why do some commodities live on one exchange and not another? And who actually guarantees that the person on the other side of your trade pays up? By the end of this lesson you will know India's four commodity exchanges, what each is known for, how a trade flows from your app to settlement, and why an exchange-traded contract is a completely different animal from a "commodity scheme" pitched on WhatsApp.

body.text: In India, commodity trading for investors means exchange-traded commodity derivatives, regulated by SEBI and guaranteed by a clearing corporation. MCX dominates metals and energy, NCDEX dominates agri, and NSE and BSE are newer, smaller entrants.

children.text: MCX handles the vast majority of commodity futures turnover in India, well over 90% by most counts. If you trade gold, silver, crude oil or copper as a retail investor, you will almost certainly be trading on MCX.

children.text: MCX: Metals and Energy

MCX, headquartered in Mumbai, is where India trades globally priced commodities. Its gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas and base metal contracts track international benchmarks converted into rupees, which is why MCX prices move overnight when US markets react to data or news.
Long trading hours.
Non-agri contracts trade from 9:00 am until late night, so Indian traders can react while COMEX and NYMEX in the US are open.
Contract sizes for every pocket.
Big contracts like 1 kg gold sit alongside Mini, Guinea and Petal versions, down to 1 gram gold contracts.
Futures and options.
Most active trading is in futures, with options on several commodities growing fast.

body.title: The MCX trading day
body.prompt: During US daylight saving time, MCX non-agri contracts trade from 9:00 am to 11:30 pm. How many hours is that trading session?
body.explanation: 9:00 am to 9:00 pm is 12 hours, and 9:00 pm to 11:30 pm adds 2.5 hours, for 14.5 hours. Compare that with NSE equity cash trading from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm, just 6 hours 15 minutes. The late session exists because crude oil and precious metals react to US market hours.

children.text: NCDEX: The Agri Exchange

markDefs.definition: Warehouses approved by the exchange, and registered with the Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA) where required, that test, grade and store commodities delivered against contracts.

children.text: NCDEX, also headquartered in Mumbai, was promoted by institutions including LIC, NABARD and NSE, and it is India's main exchange for farm commodities. Its contracts are rooted in physical trade: many settle by actual delivery of goods into
accredited warehouses
at centres near where the crop is grown and traded, such as Unjha for jeera.
Shorter hours.
Agri contracts trade during daytime hours, because the underlying mandis and physical markets operate in the day.
Delivery matters.
Quality testing, warehousing and delivery logistics are central to how NCDEX contracts work.
Policy-sensitive.
Food commodities are politically sensitive, and SEBI has suspended trading in several agri contracts to curb food inflation concerns. Chapter 5 covers this in detail.

body.text: The split between MCX and NCDEX is not arbitrary. Metals and energy are global commodities priced off international benchmarks, so they suit a late-night, globally linked exchange. Agri commodities are local, seasonal and delivery-heavy, so they suit an exchange built around warehouses and mandis.

children.text: NSE and BSE: The Newcomers

markDefs.definition: An exchange permitted to offer trading in equities, equity derivatives and commodity derivatives on one platform, under one regulator.

children.text: For years, Indian law kept stock and commodity markets apart. That changed after the FMC merged into SEBI. From October 2018, SEBI allowed a single
universal exchange
to offer both equity and commodity derivatives. NSE and BSE launched commodity segments, and MCX and NCDEX gained the right to offer equity products in turn.

In practice, liquidity in NSE and BSE commodity contracts remains thin compared with MCX. For a trader, that matters more than brand name. A contract with few buyers and sellers means wider gaps between bid and ask prices, and a higher cost every time you enter or exit.

body.title: Pick the exchange
body.question: A trader in Rajkot wants to take a futures position in jeera, based on her view of the rabi crop in Gujarat. Where is she most likely to trade?
body.explanation: Jeera futures trade on NCDEX, India's agri-focused exchange, with delivery linked to Unjha. eNAM is an electronic spot marketplace for farmers and traders, not a derivatives exchange.

children.text: How a Commodity Trade Actually Flows
When you buy one lot of MCX Gold Mini on your broker's app, several institutions do their part:
You place the order.
Your broker must be a SEBI-registered member of the exchange with the commodity segment enabled on your account.
The exchange matches it.
MCX's electronic order book pairs your buy order with a seller's order at the best available price. You never know who the seller is.
The clearing corporation steps in.
The clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer.
Margins are collected.
Both sides post margin with the clearing corporation through their brokers, and gains and losses are settled daily.
Settlement at expiry.
Depending on the contract, it settles in cash or through physical delivery via an accredited vault or warehouse.

body.label: Novation
body.value: The clearing corporation is the counterparty to every trade
body.context: If the trader on the other side of your trade defaults, the clearing corporation still pays you, backed by margins and a Settlement Guarantee Fund. This is the single biggest protection exchange trading gives you.

body.title: Who guarantees the trade?
body.textWithBlank: On an Indian commodity exchange, the ___ corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, guaranteeing settlement.
body.explanation: Clearing corporations such as MCXCCL and NCCL guarantee settlement through a process called novation. That is why you do not need to know or trust the person on the other side of your trade.

children.text: Exchange-Traded vs "Commodity Schemes": The NSEL Lesson

body.title: A SEBI-regulated exchange contract vs an unregulated commodity scheme

columns.label: Exchange-traded contract (MCX, NCDEX, NSE, BSE)
points: Settlement guaranteed by a clearing corporation
Returns depend entirely on market price, with no guarantee
Physical stock, where relevant, held in accredited vaults and warehouses

columns.label: Unregulated scheme or "spot product"
points: No clearing corporation, so counterparty risk is yours
Prices set or quoted by the promoter
Stock claims that you usually cannot verify

body.title: The NSEL crisis and what came after

events.title: NSEL begins operations
events.description: National Spot Exchange Ltd, promoted by Financial Technologies, the group that also promoted MCX, starts as a spot commodity platform outside the commodity derivatives regulator's oversight.

events.title: Paired contracts grow
events.description: Investors buy commodities for short-term settlement and simultaneously sell them for later settlement, locking in what looked like fixed returns.

events.title: Trading halts
events.description: NSEL is directed to stop launching new contracts and suspends trading. It cannot pay investors.

events.title: The default
events.description: A payment default of about ₹5,600 crore hits around 13,000 investors, and warehouse stocks turn out to be far short of what was claimed.

events.title: MCX changes hands
events.description: Financial Technologies is declared not "fit and proper" to hold a stake in a regulated exchange and exits MCX; Kotak Mahindra Bank buys a major stake.

events.title: FMC merges into SEBI
events.description: Commodity derivatives regulation moves to SEBI, with stronger rules on risk management and warehousing.

body.title: Why the "paired contract" looked safe but was not

children.text: An investor would buy, say, castor seed on NSEL for settlement in 2 days and, at the same moment, sell the same quantity for settlement around 25 to 35 days later at a higher, pre-agreed price. The spread worked out to what investors saw as a steady return of roughly 14% to 16% a year.
It looked like arbitrage, with no price risk, because both legs were locked in upfront.
In reality, the return depended entirely on the borrowers on the other side paying and on the stock actually sitting in warehouses.
There was no clearing corporation guaranteeing settlement the way there is on a regulated derivatives exchange.

When the music stopped, the stock was not there and the money could not be paid. The lesson is permanent: an "assured return" on a commodity product is a credit risk on whoever promised it, not a commodity trade.

body.text: Be very wary of any "commodity investment" offering fixed monthly returns, "arbitrage with zero risk", or physical gold or silver schemes sold through Telegram groups or private dealers. Before engaging, confirm the platform is a SEBI-recognised exchange and your broker is a SEBI-registered member of it.

body.title: The "safe silver" pitch
body.scenario: Ananya, a 34-year-old teacher in Kolkata, is added to a Telegram group called "MCX Silver Profit Club". The admin offers a "silver accumulation plan": deposit ₹50,000 by UPI to his personal account, and the club will trade MCX silver for her and pay a guaranteed 4% every month. He shares screenshots of MCX price charts and says the scheme is "backed by MCX".
body.prompt: What are the red flags, and what should Ananya check before doing anything?
body.modelAnswer:
Red flags:
1. Guaranteed returns. No exchange-traded commodity position can guarantee a return, let alone 4% a month, which compounds to roughly 60% a year.
2. Money to a personal account. Legitimate brokers never ask you to pay a person by UPI. Funds go to the broker's designated client account, linked to your own trading account.
3. "Backed by MCX". Exchanges do not back or endorse any trading scheme or tipster. MCX screenshots prove nothing.
4. Someone else trading for her. Handing trading control to an unregistered person is a classic setup for losses or outright fraud.

What to check: whether the person or entity is a SEBI-registered broker, investment adviser or research analyst on SEBI's website; whether any account would be opened in her own name with a registered broker; and whether any return is described as guaranteed, which on its own is enough to walk away.

body.title: Before you trade on any commodity exchange
steps: Confirm your broker is a SEBI-registered member of the exchange you want, such as MCX or NCDEX.
Check that the commodity derivatives segment is activated on your account. Brokers typically ask for proof of income before enabling derivatives segments.
Find the exact contract on the exchange website and read its specification: lot size, quotation, expiry and settlement type.
Check the contract's trading volume and open interest, so you know whether it is liquid.
Make sure all money moves only between your own bank account and your broker's designated account.

points: India has four commodity derivatives exchanges: MCX, NCDEX, NSE and BSE, all regulated by SEBI since the FMC merger in September 2015.
MCX dominates metals and energy, trades until late night, and handles well over 90% of commodity futures turnover.
NCDEX is the agri exchange, built around quality testing, accredited warehouses and physical delivery.
NSE and BSE added commodity segments from October 2018, but liquidity there remains thin compared with MCX.
A clearing corporation guarantees every exchange trade through novation, removing counterparty risk.
NSEL's 2013 collapse is the permanent warning: "assured returns" on commodity products are credit risk, not a commodity trade.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Exchange trading hours, contract lists and specifications change from time to time; always check the latest details on the exchange website. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin.
